findings.title: Note loop indexes past the end of fields and panics on every line
findings.detail: The loop `for index := 2; index <= len(fields); index++ { note += fields[index] }` reads fields[len(fields)] on its last pass. For a plain "item;5", len is 2 and fields[2] panics at once. With a note it panics one step later. Every non-blank line therefore crashes LoadOrder. Smallest fix: use `index < len(fields)`. Since note is thrown away anyway, simpler still is to delete the loop.

findings.title: ReserveLines bypasses Reserve: no lock, no capacity or sign check
findings.detail: ReserveLines does `stock.Reserved += line.Quantity` directly. That skips the mutex that Reserve and Free hold, which is a data race. It also skips the `Reserved+count > Capacity` check, so stock is overbooked with no error, and the positive-count check, so a negative quantity lowers Reserved. Smallest fix: call `stock.Reserve(line.Quantity)` and return its error.

findings.title: Partial reservations are left in place when a later line fails
findings.detail: Lines are reserved one at a time. If a later line names an unknown item, or fails a capacity check once F2 is fixed, the function returns an error but keeps the earlier lines' reservations. A caller that sees the error will think nothing was reserved. Fix: first check that every item exists, then reserve, and on failure undo the lines already reserved before returning.

findings.title: Quantity parse error ignored; bad quantities silently become 0 and are skipped
findings.detail: `quantity, _ := strconv.Atoi(...)` throws away the error. A typo such as "widget;1O" becomes quantity 0, and ReserveLines then skips the line without complaint, so an order line is lost unnoticed. Fix: return an error when Atoi fails, and reject quantity <= 0.

findings.title: Order file is never closed
findings.detail: LoadOrder opens the file with os.Open but never closes it, so each call leaks a file descriptor. Fix: add `defer file.Close()` right after the error check.

findings.title: ParseLine note loop indexes past the end of fields and panics on every line
findings.detail: The loop runs `for index := 2; index <= len(fields); index++` and reads fields[index]. When index equals len(fields), the read is out of range. Even a valid two-field line such as "apple;3" reads fields[2] and panics. As a result, ParseLine, and LoadOrder through it, crashes on every valid input.

findings.title: ReserveLines changes Reserved without taking the stock mutex
findings.detail: `stock.Reserved += line.Quantity` runs without stock.mutex, while Reserve and Free lock that mutex. If ReserveLines runs at the same time as Reserve, Free or another ReserveLines, the result is a data race. Updates can be lost and the reserved counts can end up wrong.

findings.title: ReserveLines skips the capacity check and overbooks stock
findings.detail: ReserveLines adds the quantity to Reserved directly instead of calling Reserve, so it never checks Reserved+count against Capacity. An order larger than the free stock still succeeds. Reserved then exceeds Capacity, and Free() goes negative.

findings.title: Negative quantities are accepted and decrease Reserved
findings.detail: ParseLine accepts any integer, including negative ones. ReserveLines skips only zero, so a line like "apple;-5" subtracts from Reserved. That releases stock other orders hold and can make Reserved negative. Reserve rejects count <= 0, but this new path does not.

findings.title: A malformed quantity is silently parsed as 0 and the line is dropped
findings.detail: ParseLine discards the error from strconv.Atoi, so text like "apple;three" or "apple;" becomes Quantity 0 with no error. ReserveLines then skips zero-quantity lines. A malformed order line is therefore lost without any error being reported.

findings.title: ReserveLines is not atomic: an error leaves earlier lines reserved
findings.detail: When a later line names an unknown item, ReserveLines returns an error but does not roll back the lines it already reserved. The caller sees the order fail while part of its stock stays reserved and leaks. If the caller retries, those lines are reserved a second time.

findings.title: LoadOrder never closes the opened file
findings.detail: os.Open is never followed by `defer file.Close()`. Every call, including the early return on a parse error, leaks a file descriptor. A long-running process that loads many orders will eventually run out of descriptors.

findings.title: Expiry check is inverted: fresh entries miss, expired entries hit
findings.detail: `if found.expires.After(cache.Now()) { return 0, false }` reports a miss while the entry is still valid, then returns the value once it has expired. As a result the cache never serves fresh data and always serves stale data, forever (entries are never evicted). Stale stock values are returned as hits, with nothing to signal they are wrong. Fix: `if !found.expires.After(cache.Now()) { return 0, false }`. Optionally delete the expired entry at that point.

findings.title: Get reads the map without the mutex, racing with Put
findings.detail: `Put` takes `cache.mutex`, but `Get` reads `cache.entries` without it. A Go map read at the same time as a write is a data race, and the runtime can crash with "concurrent map read and map write". A cache shared between goroutines will hit this. Fix: add `cache.mutex.Lock(); defer cache.mutex.Unlock()` at the top of `Get`.

findings.title: Release does not validate count, so Reserved can go negative
findings.detail: `Release` subtracts any count. A count larger than `Reserved`, for example from a double release or a release after a partial `ReserveLines` failure, makes `Reserved` negative. A negative count increases it. Either way `Free()` then reports more units than `Capacity`, and `Reserve` will oversell without anyone noticing. `Reserve` already rejects counts that are not positive. Fix: return an error when `count <= 0 || count > stock.Reserved`, mirroring `Reserve`.

findings.title: Expiry check is inverted: fresh entries are misses, expired entries are hits
findings.detail: Get returns a miss when found.expires.After(cache.Now()), which is exactly the case where the entry is still valid. Once the TTL has passed it returns the stale value as a hit. Every lookup inside the TTL misses, and every lookup after the TTL serves stale data.

findings.title: Get reads the map without taking the mutex: data race with Put
findings.detail: Put locks cache.mutex before writing cache.entries, but Get reads the map without locking. If one goroutine calls Get while another calls Put, that is a concurrent map read and write. The Go runtime can stop the program with 'concurrent map read and map write', or Get can read a corrupted entry.

findings.title: Release does not check count, so Reserved can go negative
findings.detail: Release subtracts count with no check that count is positive or no larger than Reserved. Releasing more than was reserved, releasing twice, or passing a negative count makes Reserved negative or too high. Free() then reports more units than Capacity, and later Reserve calls oversell the item. Reserve rejects bad counts, so this asymmetry is a likely source of corrupted stock.

findings.title: Expired entries are never removed, so the cache grows without bound
findings.detail: Nothing ever deletes an entry. Put only overwrites, and Get leaves expired entries in place. With many distinct keys, the map grows for the whole life of the process, which is a memory leak.

findings.title: Retry returns nil when every attempt failed
findings.detail: After the loop ends, Retry runs `return nil` instead of `return last`. When every call to work fails, the caller is told it succeeded, so the failure goes unnoticed and nobody acts on it. This contradicts the doc comment. Fix: change the final statement to `return last`.

findings.title: Shell command injection and breakage through string-built sh -c
findings.detail: Export joins pattern, stockFile and report into one string and runs it with `sh -c`. A pattern that contains a single quote, or a path with spaces or shell metacharacters such as `;`, `$()` or `>`, will break the command or run any command it contains. It can also send output to a file nobody intended, which can overwrite data. Fix: avoid the shell. Run `exec.Command("grep", "--", pattern, stockFile)`, open the report file with os.Create, set `cmd.Stdout` to it, and close it while checking the error. Alternatively, do the matching in Go.

findings.title: Last partial page is dropped
findings.detail: When `end > len(items)`, Page returns nil, so a last page holding fewer than size items is never returned. For example, 25 items with a page size of 10 gives only two pages, and items 20 to 24 are silently lost from any listing. Fix: if `start >= len(items)`, return nil; otherwise cap end with `if end > len(items) { end = len(items) }`. Also consider guarding `number*size` against overflow.

findings.title: Sleeps after the final failed attempt
findings.detail: time.Sleep(pause) runs after the last failed attempt too. This adds a pointless delay before the error is returned. Fix: sleep only when `attempt < attempts-1`.

findings.title: Shell command injection through pattern, stockFile and report
findings.detail: The command is built by joining unescaped strings into `sh -c`. A pattern containing a single quote, such as `x' /etc/passwd; rm -rf ~; echo '`, or a file name containing `;`, `$()` or spaces, lets the caller run any shell command. Even a harmless pattern like `O'Brien` makes the command fail. Run grep directly with exec.Command("grep", "--", pattern, stockFile), write its stdout to a file created with os.Create, and drop the shell.

findings.title: Retry returns nil when every attempt failed
findings.detail: After the loop the function returns nil instead of `last`, so the caller is told the work succeeded even though every call failed. This contradicts the doc comment and hides real failures. It should `return last`.

findings.title: A partial last page is returned as empty
findings.detail: When `end > len(items)` the function returns nil, so a final page with fewer than `size` items is dropped. For example, 5 items with size 2 gives page 2 = nil instead of [item4], and those items can never be reached by paging. It should cap `end` at len(items) and return nil only when start >= len(items).

findings.title: number*size can overflow and cause a slice panic
findings.detail: With a very large number or size, `start` or `end` overflows int and can become negative. A negative `end` passes the `end > len(items)` check, and slicing with negative or reversed bounds then panics. The bounds should be checked before multiplying, for example `number > len(items)/size`.

findings.title: Sleeps after the final failed attempt
findings.detail: time.Sleep(pause) also runs after the last attempt, which delays the caller by a full pause for nothing before it returns. The function should skip the sleep when attempt == attempts-1.

findings.title: Note loop indexes past end of fields and panics on every line
findings.detail: The loop `for index := 2; index <= len(fields); index++` reads fields[len(fields)], which is out of range. With a plain "item;quantity" line (len 2) it reads fields[2] right away, and with a note it panics after the last field. Every non-blank line therefore panics with index out of range, so LoadOrder crashes on any real order file. The condition should be `index < len(fields)`.

findings.title: ReserveLines skips the capacity check and overbooks stock
findings.detail: ReserveLines adds line.Quantity straight to stock.Reserved without checking it against Capacity, unlike Reserve, which returns ErrNotEnough. An order can reserve more units than exist, so Free() goes negative and the item is oversold.

findings.title: Data race: Reserved is modified without holding the mutex
findings.detail: ReserveLines writes stock.Reserved without taking stock.mutex, while Reserve and Free lock it. If ReserveLines runs at the same time as Reserve or Free, or as another ReserveLines call, this is a data race and updates can be lost or read torn. It should go through Reserve or lock the mutex.

findings.title: Bad quantity is silently parsed as 0 and the line is dropped
findings.detail: The error from strconv.Atoi is ignored, so a quantity like "abc" or "1O" becomes 0 and ParseLine still returns no error. ReserveLines then skips lines with quantity 0, so a mistyped line vanishes from the order with no error reported.

findings.title: Negative quantities are accepted and lower Reserved
findings.detail: Nothing rejects a negative quantity: ParseLine accepts "item;-5", and ReserveLines only skips 0. ReserveLines then adds -5 to Reserved, which releases units someone else holds and can push Reserved below zero, raising Free() above Capacity. Reserve rejects count <= 0, but ReserveLines does not.

findings.title: A failure partway through leaves earlier lines reserved
findings.detail: When a later line names an unknown item, ReserveLines returns an error after it has already added the earlier lines to their stocks, and it never rolls them back. The caller sees the order as failed, but stock stays reserved for it with no record, so those units leak, and a retry reserves them again.

findings.title: Order file is never closed
findings.detail: LoadOrder opens the file with os.Open but never calls Close: there is no defer, and the early returns on parse errors skip any cleanup too. Each call leaks a file descriptor, and a long-running service that loads many orders eventually hits the open-file limit.

findings.title: Note loop indexes past the end of the slice, so every line panics
findings.detail: The loop is `for index := 2; index <= len(fields); index++ { note += fields[index] }`. It reads fields[len(fields)], which is out of range. With the minimal input "item;3", len is 2 and fields[2] panics. Every line that gets past the length check therefore crashes, and so does LoadOrder. Smallest fix: use `index < len(fields)`, or remove the unused note code entirely (note is thrown away with `_ = note`).

findings.title: ReserveLines bypasses Stock.Reserve: no capacity check, no positive-count check, no lock
findings.detail: `stock.Reserved += line.Quantity` changes the field directly. It skips the capacity check, so Reserved can go above Capacity and Free() goes negative without any error. Negative quantities lower Reserved. The write happens without stock.mutex, so it races with Reserve and Free. Smallest fix: call `stock.Reserve(line.Quantity)` and return its error. If an order should be all-or-nothing, also release the lines already reserved when a later line fails (see F4).

findings.title: Quantity parse error is ignored, so bad lines become quantity 0 and are silently skipped
findings.detail: `quantity, _ := strconv.Atoi(...)` throws away the error. A typo such as "widget;1O" or "widget;" turns into Quantity 0. ReserveLines then `continue`s past it, so that order line is dropped with no error. Negative values are also accepted. Fix: return an error when Atoi fails, and when the quantity is not positive.

findings.title: A failure partway through leaves the earlier lines reserved
findings.detail: When an item is unknown (or, once F2 is fixed, a line doesn't fit), ReserveLines returns an error. The lines already processed stay reserved, and the caller has no way to tell which ones. Fix: check that every item exists before reserving anything. Then, if a Reserve call fails, release what this order already reserved and return the error.

findings.title: LoadOrder never closes the file
findings.detail: The file returned by os.Open is never closed, so each call leaks one file descriptor. Fix: add `defer file.Close()` after the error check.

findings.title: Expiry check is inverted: live entries are misses, expired entries are hits
findings.detail: Get returns a miss when found.expires.After(Now()), i.e. while the entry is still valid, and returns the value once it has expired. The cache never serves fresh values and always serves stale ones. The condition should be !found.expires.After(cache.Now()).

findings.title: Get reads the map without taking the mutex, racing with Put
findings.detail: Put locks cache.mutex before writing cache.entries, but Get reads cache.entries without locking. A Get running at the same time as a Put is a data race on a Go map. The runtime can abort the process with 'concurrent map read and map write'.

findings.title: Release does not validate count, so Reserved can go negative
findings.detail: Release subtracts count with no check. It accepts a non-positive count, and a count larger than Reserved (a double release or a release of an over-large amount) drives Reserved below zero. Free() then reports more units than Capacity, and later reservations can oversell the stock. Reserve rejects count<=0, but Release has no matching check and does not reject releasing more than is reserved.

findings.title: Expired entries are never removed, so the cache grows without bound
findings.detail: Nothing deletes entries: Get leaves expired entries in place, and there is no eviction or size limit. With many distinct keys the map keeps growing and leaks memory over the life of the process.

findings.title: Cache.Get expiry check is inverted: serves only stale values
findings.detail: Get returns a miss when `found.expires.After(cache.Now())`, which is true when the entry is still valid. It returns the value only after the TTL has passed. Every fresh lookup misses, and every expired value is returned as a hit with no warning, so callers act on old data. Fix: return a miss when `!found.expires.After(cache.Now())`, i.e. when `cache.Now()` is not before `expires`.

findings.title: Cache.Get reads the map without the mutex
findings.detail: Put locks `cache.mutex` before writing `entries`, but Get reads `cache.entries[key]` without the lock. A Get running at the same time as a Put is a data race on a Go map. The runtime can abort the process with a fatal 'concurrent map read and map write' error, and recover() cannot catch it. A shared lookup cache is used concurrently by design. Fix: add `cache.mutex.Lock(); defer cache.mutex.Unlock()` at the top of Get.

findings.title: Release does not validate count, so Reserved can go negative
findings.detail: Release subtracts count with no checks. A zero or negative count, or a count larger than Reserved (for example a duplicate release on a retried cancel), leaves Reserved negative or wrong. A negative Reserved makes Free() larger than Capacity, so Reserve accepts more units than exist and stock is oversold without anyone noticing. Reserve already rejects count <= 0. Fix: return an error, matching Reserve, when count <= 0 or count > stock.Reserved, and only subtract after those checks pass.

findings.title: Shell command injection via pattern, stockFile and report
findings.detail: Export builds a string for `sh -c` by joining pattern, stockFile and report without escaping. A pattern holding a single quote (e.g. `x'; rm -rf ~; echo '`) or file names with spaces, `;`, `$()` or backticks run arbitrary commands, and names with spaces break the call. Run grep directly with exec.Command("grep", "--", pattern, stockFile) and write its stdout to a file opened with os.Create(report), with no shell.

findings.title: Retry returns nil when every attempt fails
findings.detail: The function ends with `return nil` instead of `return last`. When all attempts fail, callers see success and go on as if the work was done, for example as if stock had been reserved or released. This contradicts the doc comment, which says the last error is returned.

findings.title: The last, partial page is dropped
findings.detail: When end > len(items), Page returns nil instead of clamping end to len(items). For 25 items with size 10, page 2 comes back empty, so the last 5 items can never be reached. When the item count is smaller than the page size, page 0 is empty too. Fix: return nil only when start >= len(items), and otherwise set end = min(end, len(items)).

findings.title: Retry sleeps after the final failed attempt
findings.detail: time.Sleep(pause) runs after every failure, including the last one. The caller waits one extra pause for nothing before getting the result.

findings.title: number*size can overflow and cause a panic
findings.detail: With very large number or size values, start := number*size or end := start+size wraps around to a negative or small value. That passes the end > len check and gives an out-of-range or inverted slice, which panics. Check start against len(items) with division, or bound number before multiplying.

findings.title: Retry returns nil after every attempt has failed
findings.detail: After the loop the function returns `nil` instead of `last`, so a failure that persists through all attempts looks like success. Callers carry on as if the work completed, and nobody notices. This contradicts the doc comment, which says the last error is returned. Fix: `return last`. Also skip `time.Sleep(pause)` after the final attempt, which only adds a needless wait. When attempts <= 0, return an error rather than nil.

findings.title: Shell command built by string joining: injection and breakage on quotes and spaces
findings.detail: `sh -c "grep '"+pattern+"' "+stockFile+" > "+report` puts unescaped input into a shell command line. Any pattern containing `'` breaks the quoting: an ordinary name like O'Brien fails, and a crafted pattern such as `'; rm -rf ~; '` runs arbitrary commands. Also note that grep exits with status 1 when nothing matches, so Export returns an error for an empty result. Treat exit status 1 as success.

A pattern that contains a single quote (for example `x'; rm -rf ~; echo '`) ends the quoted argument and runs any command. File names with spaces, `;`, `$()` or backticks are also read by the shell. Even a harmless item name with an apostrophe, such as `O'Brien`, breaks the command. Run grep with exec.Command("grep", "--", pattern, stockFile) and separate arguments instead, and write its stdout to a file opened with os.Create, or filter the lines in Go.

findings.title: Retry returns nil when every attempt failed
findings.detail: When every call fails, the loop ends and the function returns `nil` instead of `last`. Callers see success after the work failed, so the failure is lost and the caller goes on as if, for example, stock had been reserved or written. The same happens when attempts <= 0, because work never runs and nil comes back. The function should return `last`, and should return an error when attempts <= 0.

findings.title: Retry sleeps needlessly after the final failed attempt
findings.detail: time.Sleep(pause) runs after every failure, including the last one. Every call that fails completely is held up for one extra pause before it returns. Sleep only when another attempt will follow.

findings.title: Last partial page is dropped
findings.detail: When end > len(items), Page returns nil instead of clamping end to len(items). Unless the item count is an exact multiple of size, the items on the last page can never be reached: 5 items with size 2 give pages 0 and 1, but page 2 (the 5th item) comes back nil. A list shorter than size returns nil even for page 0. Return nil only when start >= len(items), and otherwise set end = min(end, len(items)).

findings.title: number*size can overflow for very large page numbers
findings.detail: start := number * size has no overflow check. With very large number or size values taken from user input, start or end can wrap around to a negative value. Slicing with a negative or reversed bound then panics, for example when end wraps negative while start stays positive. Compare number against len(items)/size before multiplying.

findings.title: Note loop indexes past end of fields, panicking on every line
findings.detail: The loop runs `for index := 2; index <= len(fields); index++` and reads fields[index]. When index == len(fields) this is out of range, so any line with 2 or more fields, which means every valid line, panics with index out of range. The bound should be `<`.

findings.title: ReserveLines writes Reserved without taking the stock mutex
findings.detail: `stock.Reserved += line.Quantity` runs without stock.mutex, while Reserve and Free lock it. Calls that run at the same time as Reserve or Free, or another ReserveLines, race on Reserved. Updates can be lost and the counts can be corrupted.

findings.title: ReserveLines skips the capacity check and over-reserves
findings.detail: Unlike Reserve, ReserveLines adds the quantity without checking Reserved+count <= Capacity and never returns ErrNotEnough. An order can reserve more units than exist, which leaves Free() negative.

findings.title: Negative quantities are accepted and reduce Reserved
findings.detail: Only Quantity == 0 is skipped. A negative quantity from the order file is added to Reserved, which lowers it and frees stock that other orders hold, possibly below zero. Reserve rejects count <= 0, but this path does not.

findings.title: Partial reservation is not rolled back on error
findings.detail: When a later line names an unknown item, the function returns an error after earlier lines have already been added to their stocks. The caller sees a failed order, but those units stay reserved and leak.

findings.title: Invalid quantity is silently parsed as 0
findings.detail: The error from strconv.Atoi is discarded, so a malformed quantity such as 'abc' or '5x' becomes 0 and no error is returned. ReserveLines then skips the line, so a corrupt order passes as if it were valid.

findings.title: Opened order file is never closed
findings.detail: os.Open is not followed by defer file.Close(). Every call leaks a file descriptor, on success and on the early-return error path alike, and enough calls exhaust the process's descriptors.

findings.title: Note loop indexes past the end of fields and panics on every valid line
findings.detail: The loop runs `for index := 2; index <= len(fields); index++` and reads `fields[index]`. When index == len(fields) that is out of range. For a plain "item;3" line, fields has length 2, so fields[2] panics. With a note it still reaches fields[len] and panics. Every valid input line crashes, and so LoadOrder crashes too. Fix: use `index < len(fields)`, or just drop the note loop, since the note is thrown away anyway.

findings.title: ReserveLines skips Reserve: no lock, no capacity check, negatives accepted
findings.detail: ReserveLines changes stock.Reserved directly instead of calling stock.Reserve. It does not take stock.mutex, so it races with Reserve and Free. It never checks against Capacity, so it can overbook and push Free below zero without any error. It also accepts negative quantities, which lower Reserved and so release stock that was never reserved. Fix: call `stock.Reserve(line.Quantity)` and return its error. Reject quantities that are not positive at parse time rather than skipping them.

findings.title: Partial reservation is left in place when a later line fails
findings.detail: If a later line names an unknown item, or would fail once capacity is checked, the reservations already made for earlier lines are never undone. The order ends up half reserved even though the function returns an error. Fix: check every line first (item exists and quantity fits), then apply them all. Or keep track of what was applied and roll it back on error. Either way, hold the locks needed to make the change atomic.

findings.title: Error from strconv.Atoi is ignored, so a bad quantity silently becomes 0
findings.detail: `quantity, _ := strconv.Atoi(...)` throws away the parse error. A line such as "widget;ten" or "widget;" becomes Quantity 0, and ReserveLines then quietly skips it, so an order line is lost with no error. Fix: return an error naming the line when Atoi fails. Also reject quantities that are not positive.

findings.title: Order file is never closed
findings.detail: LoadOrder opens the file with os.Open but never closes it, so a file descriptor leaks on every call, including the early-return error path. Fix: add `defer file.Close()` right after the error check on os.Open.

findings.title: Expiry check inverted: fresh entries miss, expired entries hit
findings.detail: Get returns (0,false) when found.expires.After(cache.Now()), i.e. while the entry is still valid, and returns the value once it has expired. So the cache never returns a fresh value, and it serves stale values forever after the TTL. The condition should be !found.expires.After(now), or now.After(expires).

findings.title: Get reads the map without holding the mutex (data race)
findings.detail: Put locks cache.mutex before writing entries, but Get reads cache.entries without locking. If Get and Put run at the same time, that is a data race on a Go map, and the runtime can abort with 'concurrent map read and map write'.

findings.title: Release does not validate count, so Reserved can go negative
findings.detail: Release subtracts count with no checks. A non-positive count, or a count larger than Reserved (for example a double release), drives Reserved negative or raises it. Free() then reports more units than Capacity, and later reservations oversell the stock. Reserve rejects count <= 0, but Release has no matching guard.

findings.title: Expired entries are never evicted (unbounded growth)
findings.detail: Nothing ever deletes an entry. Get does not remove an expired one, and there is no sweep. A cache that sees many distinct keys keeps growing in memory for as long as the process runs.

findings.title: Cache.Get expiry check is inverted: fresh entries miss, expired entries hit
findings.detail: `if found.expires.After(cache.Now()) { return 0, false }` treats an entry that has not expired yet as a miss, then returns the value once it has expired. Every lookup inside the TTL misses, and every lookup after it returns stale data with ok=true and no warning. That is the opposite of what the doc comment promises. Fix: return a miss when `!found.expires.After(cache.Now())`, i.e. when the entry has expired.

findings.title: Cache.Get reads the map without holding the mutex
findings.detail: `Put` locks `cache.mutex`, but `Get` reads `cache.entries` without locking. Calling Get and Put at the same time is a data race, and Go can crash with 'concurrent map read and map write'. Fix: start Get with `cache.mutex.Lock(); defer cache.mutex.Unlock()`.

findings.title: Release does not validate count, so Reserved can go negative
findings.detail: `Release` subtracts `count` without any checks. Releasing more than is reserved (for example a double release) or passing a negative count makes `Reserved` negative or larger than `Capacity`. `Free()` then reports more units than exist, and `Reserve` will oversell without any error. `Reserve` already rejects counts that are not positive. Fix: return an error when `count <= 0 || count > stock.Reserved`, and otherwise subtract.

findings.title: Shell command injection through pattern, stockFile and report
findings.detail: Export builds a string that runs through `sh -c` by joining pattern, stockFile and report together. A pattern that contains a single quote (for example `x'; rm -rf ~; echo '`) breaks out of the quoting. Paths with spaces or shell metacharacters are also run as shell syntax. Either can execute any command the caller's input supplies. Use exec.Command("grep", "--", pattern, stockFile) and write its stdout to a file opened in Go instead.

findings.title: Retry returns nil when every attempt failed
findings.detail: Inside the loop the function saves each error in `last`, but after the loop it returns nil instead of `last`. When work fails on every attempt, the caller is told it succeeded, which contradicts the doc comment and hides the failure. It should return last.

findings.title: Last partial page is dropped
findings.detail: When end > len(items), Page returns nil instead of clamping end to len(items). For example, with 25 items and size 10, page 2 should hold items 20 to 24 but comes back empty. Any list whose length is not a multiple of size loses its trailing items. Clamp end, and return nil only when start >= len(items).

findings.title: Sleeps after the final failed attempt
findings.detail: time.Sleep(pause) runs even after the last attempt, when no further call will follow. Every fully failed retry is delayed by one extra pause for no reason.

findings.title: No match is reported as an error
findings.detail: grep exits with status 1 when no line matches, so Export returns an *exec.ExitError for a valid export that finds nothing. Callers cannot tell that case apart from a real failure, such as a missing stock file, which gives exit status 2.

findings.title: Retry returns nil when every attempt fails
findings.detail: After the loop ends, Retry returns nil instead of `last`. When every call fails, the caller is told the work succeeded and never sees the error. This contradicts the doc comment. Fix: `return last`. Also, the function sleeps after the final failed attempt for no reason. Skip the sleep when `attempt == attempts-1`.

findings.title: Shell command injection through pattern, stockFile and report
findings.detail: Export runs `sh -c` on a command built by joining the three inputs into one string. A pattern that contains a single quote breaks out of the quoting. It can run arbitrary commands, and an ordinary search like `O'Brien` also breaks the command. Unquoted file names with spaces or shell metacharacters break the command or are interpreted by the shell. Through `report`, a caller can redirect output to any path. Fix: don't use the shell. Run `exec.Command("grep", "-e", pattern, "--", stockFile)`, set its Stdout to an `os.Create(report)` file, or filter the lines in Go. Also note that grep exits with status 1 when nothing matches, so Export returns an error for an empty result that should not count as a failure. Treat exit code 1 as success.

findings.title: Last partial page is dropped
findings.detail: When `end > len(items)`, Page returns nil instead of clamping `end`. Whenever the item count is not a multiple of the page size, the last items can never be shown, and nothing signals that they are missing. For example, 25 items with size 10 gives an empty page 2. Fix: return nil only if `start >= len(items)`, and otherwise set `end = min(end, len(items))`. A large page number can also make `number*size` overflow. Guard by checking `number > len(items)/size` first.

findings.title: ParseLine indexes past the end of fields and panics on every valid line
findings.detail: The note loop runs `for index := 2; index <= len(fields); index++` and reads fields[index]. On the last pass index equals len(fields), which is out of range. For an ordinary line "item;3", len(fields) is 2, so the code reads fields[2] and panics. Every non-blank line in an order file has at least two fields, so every one of them crashes ParseLine and LoadOrder, and the process goes down with it. Fix: use `index < len(fields)`. Since note is thrown away anyway, the simpler fix is to delete the loop.

findings.title: ReserveLines bypasses the mutex and the capacity check, so it can oversell
findings.detail: ReserveLines runs `stock.Reserved += line.Quantity` directly. It does not take stock.mutex and does not check against Capacity. An order larger than the free stock goes through without error, Reserved ends up above Capacity, and Free() returns a negative number. Running it at the same time as Reserve or Free is a data race and can lose updates. Negative quantities pass straight through and lower Reserved. Fix: call stock.Reserve(line.Quantity) for each line and return its error.

findings.title: Bad or negative quantity is silently accepted
findings.detail: `quantity, _ := strconv.Atoi(...)` ignores the parse error. A typo such as "widget;1O" becomes quantity 0, and ReserveLines then skips that line, so the order is quietly under-reserved and nobody is told. Negative values such as "-5" also pass. Fix: return the Atoi error, and reject quantity <= 0 with an error.

findings.title: ReserveLines leaves earlier lines reserved when a later line fails
findings.detail: When a later line names an unknown item, or fails a capacity check once F2 is fixed, ReserveLines returns an error but the reservations for earlier lines stay in place. A caller that sees the error and treats the order as rejected leaks those reserved units. Fix: either check every line before reserving anything, or roll back the lines already reserved before returning the error. Document whichever behaviour you choose.

findings.title: LoadOrder never closes the file
findings.detail: LoadOrder opens the file with os.Open but never closes it, so each call leaks a file descriptor. In a long-running process that loads many orders, this ends in 'too many open files'. Fix: add `defer file.Close()` right after the error check.

findings.title: ParseLine note loop indexes past end of slice and panics on every line
findings.detail: The loop runs `for index := 2; index <= len(fields); index++` and reads fields[index]. When index equals len(fields), that read is out of range. For a plain "item;3" line, len(fields) is 2, so fields[2] is read right away and the code panics. With a note, the last pass also goes past the end. Every valid line crashes ParseLine and LoadOrder. The condition should be `index < len(fields)`.

findings.title: ReserveLines changes Reserved without taking the stock mutex
findings.detail: `stock.Reserved += line.Quantity` runs without stock.mutex, while Reserve and Free lock it. Running this at the same time as Reserve, Free or another ReserveLines is a data race. Updates can be lost and the reservation count can become wrong.

findings.title: ReserveLines skips the capacity check and overbooks stock
findings.detail: Unlike Reserve, ReserveLines never checks Reserved+Quantity against Capacity and never returns ErrNotEnough. An order larger than the free stock still succeeds, so Reserved can exceed Capacity and Free() goes negative.

findings.title: Negative quantities are accepted and reduce Reserved
findings.detail: ParseLine accepts any integer and ReserveLines only skips 0. A line like "apple;-5" lowers Reserved, which releases stock that other orders hold and can push Reserved below zero. Reserve rejects count <= 0, but this path does not.

findings.title: Quantity parse error ignored; malformed quantity silently becomes 0 and line is skipped
findings.detail: The error from strconv.Atoi is thrown away, so a bad quantity such as "abc", "" or "2.5" becomes 0 with no error. ReserveLines then skips any line with quantity 0, so a corrupt order line is dropped silently and is not reported.

findings.title: ReserveLines is not atomic: partial reservations remain when it fails partway
findings.detail: When an item is unknown, ReserveLines returns an error after the earlier lines are already added to their stocks, and nothing rolls them back. The caller sees a failed order but stock stays reserved for part of it. A retry reserves those lines a second time.

findings.title: LoadOrder never closes the opened file
findings.detail: The file from os.Open is never closed: there is no `defer file.Close()`. Each call leaks a file descriptor until the GC runs the finalizer. If many orders are loaded, the process can run out of descriptors.

findings.title: Expiry check is inverted: fresh entries miss, expired entries hit
findings.detail: `Get` returns a miss when `found.expires.After(cache.Now())`, which is true exactly while the entry is still valid. Once the TTL has passed, it returns the cached value as a hit. Every fresh lookup misses the cache, and every expired one silently serves a stale value indefinitely, so inventory decisions are made on outdated numbers without anyone noticing. Fix: return a miss when `!found.expires.After(cache.Now())`, i.e. when `Now` is at or past `expires`.

findings.title: Get reads the entries map without holding the mutex
findings.detail: `Put` takes `cache.mutex` before writing `cache.entries`, but `Get` reads the map with no lock. When `Get` and `Put` run concurrently, Go's runtime can abort with "concurrent map read and map write", and at minimum it is a data race. The whole point of a mutex-guarded cache is concurrent use, so this will happen in normal operation. Fix: call `cache.mutex.Lock(); defer cache.mutex.Unlock()` at the start of `Get`.

findings.title: Release does not validate count, so Reserved can go negative or grow
findings.detail: `Release` subtracts `count` with no checks. Releasing more than is reserved (for example a double release, or releasing a line that never got reserved) drives `Reserved` below zero. `Free()` then reports more than `Capacity`, and `Reserve` lets you take more units than physically exist. A negative `count` instead increases `Reserved`, bypassing the capacity check in `Reserve`. Fix: mirror `Reserve` by rejecting `count <= 0` and `count > stock.Reserved` with an error (and change the signature to return `error`).

findings.title: Expiry check inverted: live entries miss, expired entries hit
findings.detail: Get returns a miss when found.expires.After(Now()), i.e. while the entry is still valid, and returns the value once it has expired. Every lookup within the TTL misses, and every lookup after the TTL returns stale data indefinitely. The condition should be !found.expires.After(cache.Now()) (or Now().After/Equal expires).

findings.title: Get reads the map without taking the mutex
findings.detail: Put locks cache.mutex but Get reads cache.entries unlocked. A concurrent Get and Put is a data race on a Go map, which can trigger the runtime fatal error 'concurrent map read and map write' and crash the process, or return torn entries. Get must lock the mutex the same way Put does.

findings.title: Release accepts any count, so Reserved can go negative
findings.detail: Release subtracts count with no validation. Releasing more than is reserved (for example a double release or a wrong quantity) or passing a negative count drives Reserved below 0 or above Capacity. A negative Reserved makes Free() report more than Capacity and lets later Reserve calls oversell stock. Reserve rejects count <= 0, but Release has no matching guard and no check that count <= Reserved.

findings.title: Expired entries are never evicted
findings.detail: Nothing removes entries from cache.entries: Get does not delete expired entries and there is no sweep. With many distinct keys the map grows without bound, which is a memory leak in a long-running process.

findings.title: Shell command injection through pattern, stockFile and report
findings.detail: Export runs `sh -c "grep '"+pattern+"' "+stockFile+" > "+report`. A pattern that contains a single quote breaks out of the quoting. This can happen by accident with item names such as O'Brien, or on purpose with input like `x'; rm -rf ~; '`. Either way the shell runs arbitrary commands. A file path that contains spaces or `;`, `$()` and similar characters is just as unsafe. Smallest fix: drop the shell. Run `exec.Command("grep", "-e", pattern, "--", stockFile)`, open the report file with os.Create, and set it as cmd.Stdout. Even simpler, filter the lines in Go with bufio and strings.Contains or regexp. Also note that grep exits with status 1 when nothing matches. Decide whether no matches should be an error.

findings.title: Retry returns nil even when every attempt failed
findings.detail: After the loop, the function ends with `return nil` instead of `return last`. This contradicts the doc comment, which says it returns the last error. Callers will treat a permanent failure as success, and the wrong result passes unnoticed. Fix: `return last`. Separately, the loop sleeps after the final failed attempt, which wastes `pause` for nothing. Skip the sleep when `attempt == attempts-1`. Also decide whether attempts <= 0 should return an error instead of nil.

findings.title: Last partial page is dropped
findings.detail: When `end > len(items)`, Page returns nil. With 25 items and size 10, page 2 should hold items 20–24 but comes back empty. Any caller that pages until it gets an empty page silently loses the trailing items. Fix: return nil only when `start >= len(items)`, and otherwise clamp `end = min(end, len(items))`. The multiplication `number*size` can also overflow for huge inputs. Comparing `number > len(items)/size` first avoids that.

findings.title: Shell command injection via pattern, stockFile and report
findings.detail: The pattern and file names are concatenated into a string run by `sh -c`. A pattern containing a single quote (e.g. `x' ; rm -rf ~ ; '`) or a file name with spaces or metacharacters ends the quoting and runs arbitrary commands. Even harmless inputs like an item named O'Brien break the command. Call exec.Command("grep", "--", pattern, stockFile) directly and write its stdout to a file opened with os.Create.

findings.title: Retry returns nil when every attempt failed
findings.detail: After the loop the function returns nil instead of `last`. Callers are told the work succeeded when every call failed, so the failures are silently lost. It should return `last`.

findings.title: Last partial page is dropped
findings.detail: When the last page holds fewer than size items, end > len(items) and the function returns nil. For example, 5 items with size 2 make page 2 empty, so the 5th item can never be reached. `end` should be clamped to len(items), and nil returned only when start >= len(items).

findings.title: Needless sleep after the final failed attempt
findings.detail: time.Sleep(pause) also runs after the last attempt, so a call that has already failed in full waits one extra pause before it returns.

findings.title: Integer overflow in number*size can panic on slicing
findings.detail: With a very large number or size, number*size or start+size can wrap to a negative value. end then passes the `end > len` check, and items[start:end] panics with indices out of range. Validate the arguments with division, or check that start < len(items) without multiplying.
